script.title: Consignment vs Joint Venture
script.caption_hook: Agent or partner-like? Consignment vs Joint Venture in one minute

lines.say: Consignment and joint venture sound so similar. Agent or partner?
Good question! Both involve two parties working together, but the relationship is different. Let's see how.
Okay, so what exactly is consignment?
The consignor sends goods to a consignee to sell on his behalf. The consignor stays owner until a customer buys.
Wait, so the consignee owns the goods he holds?
No. He is only an agent. The consignee earns commission on sales and does not bear the consignment's profit or loss.
Hmm, got it. And joint venture?
Two or more co-venturers carry out one particular venture together. They share profit or loss in an agreed ratio.
So it's basically a partnership firm?
Partner-like, but not a firm. It usually ends when the venture is complete. Consignment continues, with many consignments.
Can you put them side by side?
Sure! The consignee earns commission. Co-venturers share the result in their agreed ratio.
Oh! Commission means consignment, profit ratio means joint venture!
Exactly! C for Commission, J for Join.

check_notes: Writer: Versus cards now both name the person (Consignee / Venturer) because card titles are limited to 10 characters; 'Co-venturer' would not fit. The consignee line now says commission on sales and no share of profit or loss.

Checker: Line 10 (voice): 'Consignment continues, with many consignments' is loosely worded and sounds like a rule that every consignment must continue. Better: 'A consignment relationship can carry on over many consignments, while a joint venture usually ends when its one venture is complete.'

Checker: Line 6 (voice and board 'Bears no profit or loss'): this is true for an ordinary consignee, but a consignee paid del credere commission does bear the loss from bad debts. Better: 'An ordinary consignee does not bear the profit or loss on the consignment; with del credere commission, he bears bad debts.'
Checker: Line 2 (voice): 'Both involve two parties' doesn't fit a joint venture, which can have two or more co-venturers, as Line 8 itself says. Better: 'Both involve parties working together.'
